URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611205946
Iran International, 20 November 2026

Under the agreement, brokered by senior Shiite political leaders, Kataib Hezbollah fighters would relocate from Jurf al-Sakhar to other areas, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, told Reuters.

The deal follows days of escalating tensions after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered preparations for government forces to take control of Jurf al-Sakhar, a Kataib Hezbollah stronghold in Babil province, about 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad.

Al Arabiya separately reported, citing sources, that the agreement provides for a phased withdrawal of the militia within a month, alongside the deployment of Iraqi security forces.

The militia warned Tuesday that it would resist any attempt by government forces to enter the area, which it has controlled for more than a decade.

The dispute intensified after Iraqi authorities investigated allegations that Kataib Hezbollah operated an oil-smuggling network that diverted hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, Reuters reported. The militia denied the allegations.

Esmail Qaani, commander of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse the standoff, according to Iraqi Shiite political sources cited by Reuters.

A Kataib Hezbollah spokesperson said the group's leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani, Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri and other figures in talks aimed at preventing a confrontation. Participants described the outcome as positive Thursday.

Iraq also announced that a joint security command would begin operating in Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, bringing together army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilization Forces units.

Iraqi armed forces were placed on heightened alert Thursday ahead of the deployment, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency.

Kataib Hezbollah subsequently ordered its fighters to resume normal duties after days of heightened tensions, according to a statement by the group's leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi.

The standoff has tested Zaidi's efforts to bring Iran-backed militias under state authority. Kataib Hezbollah operates within Iraq's officially recognized Popular Mobilization Forces but has frequently challenged government authority.

The United States has designated Kataib Hezbollah a foreign terrorist organization since 2009.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesIran war could cut global oil demand by over 4% by 2035 - IEANov 20, 2026, 00:04 GMT+0Listen to this article100%Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf. (ISNA)Global energy markets may never return to their pre-war structure if disruption to the Strait of Hormuz persists, while energy-security responses to the Iran war could cut global oil demand by more than 4% by 2035, the International Energy Agency said Thursday.

The conflict has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of natural gas supplies from the Persian Gulf, according to the agency's World Energy Outlook 2026.

The Strait of Hormuz normally carries about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, making it a critical route for energy exports from the Persian Gulf.

“The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system. While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said.

Hormuz disruption could redirect global oil trade

Under its Low Hormuz Case, which examines prolonged shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz, the IEA said investments in alternative pipelines, new supply sources and measures to reduce oil demand could reduce the need for oil flows through the waterway from 20 million barrels per day before the crisis to 8.5 million by 2030 and less than 2 million by 2035.

The case is not a forecast but explores how energy markets could adapt if significant risks to shipping through Hormuz persist.

Even under that scenario, the Middle East would remain the world's largest oil-exporting region, the report said.

Energy security drives shift toward domestic supplies

The IEA said the crisis was prompting governments to reconsider energy security strategies, with renewable energy, particularly solar power, and nuclear power among the potential beneficiaries of efforts to reduce reliance on imported fuels.

Under its Additional Response Case, which examines stronger government measures to improve energy security, global oil demand would fall to 97 million barrels per day by 2035, about 4.4 million barrels per day below the agency's Stated Policies Scenario, which reflects governments' current policy intentions.

Global natural gas demand would also be more than 300 billion cubic metres lower under the Additional Response Case than under the Stated Policies Scenario.

Across its exploratory scenarios, the IEA projected faster growth in electricity demand through 2035, with electricity's share of global final energy consumption approaching 30%.

However, the IEA said energy security concerns could also encourage some Asian countries to rely on domestic coal resources for longer.

Higher fuel prices and supply shortages could undermine progress in expanding access to electricity and clean cooking, particularly in developing economies, the agency said.

The outlook also examined the possibility of a recovery in oil and natural gas supplies if the war ends and shipping disruptions ease, potentially creating a buyer's market and putting downward pressure on energy prices.

The agency said prolonged uncertainty over the war and shipping through Hormuz would make governments more likely to turn their emerging preferences for diversified supplies, domestic energy resources and electrification into lasting policy changes.

Listen to this article100%View of the damage (left) to the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund (pictured in the right), following a Houthi attack in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, November 19, 2026. A missile attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis damaged Riyadh’s tallest building on Thursday, blowing out windows at the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in the second attack on the capital’s financial district this month.

Saudi Civil Defense said the attack damaged several floors of the Public Investment Fund Tower and nearby buildings. No one was injured. Residents heard a blast before dawn, and a Reuters witness saw people being evacuated from the King Abdullah Financial District, where entrances were closed and ambulances and fire trucks had gathered.

Three people familiar with the incident told Reuters a Houthi missile struck the tower directly. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said its initial assessment pointed to damage from falling debris after it responded to a missile fired toward Riyadh. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for Thursday’s attack.

Qatar and Jordan condemned the attacks on civilian and economic facilities in Riyadh. Qatar’s foreign ministry backed Saudi Arabia’s right to take legitimate measures to protect its territory and citizens. Jordan said the strikes violated Saudi sovereignty, international law and the UN Charter.

Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jasem al-Budaiwi urged the UN Security Council to hold the Houthis accountable for attacks on civilians. Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry called on the council’s permanent members to enforce existing resolutions and said the kingdom reserved the right to defend itself.

The 385-meter tower houses the fund at the center of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s drive to diversify the Saudi economy beyond oil. An attack on November 8 damaged a building belonging to state oil company Aramco in the same district.

On Wednesday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had fired cruise missiles at Riyadh’s international airport and financial district. The Saudi-led coalition said that day it had intercepted two drones, one in the Riyadh region and another in the south. It also reported airstrikes on Houthi missile depots and drone workshops in Yemen. Houthi-run media reported further Saudi strikes on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, early Thursday.

The exchanges came as Saudi officials warned allies that the campaign in Yemen could last another six months, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The officials said Riyadh wanted forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government to regain ground before entering negotiations with the Houthis.

Listen to this article100%A photo of two commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz released by Iran's semi-official ISNA on Nov. 16, 2026.Iran is considering resuming oil exports in defiance of the US naval blockade, a Revolutionary Guards-affiliated outlet reported Thursday, hours after a ship-tracking service said Iran appeared to be preparing to ship crude again for the first time in four months.

In a post labeled “unofficial,” the IRGC-affiliated Sabereen News said dozens of Iranian tankers were preparing to set sail for China.

TankerTrackers co-founder Samir Madani told Reuters that one tanker was taking on Iranian crude from another vessel in the Persian Gulf on Thursday. If it cleared the blockade, he said, it would be the first successful seaborne export of Iranian crude since mid-July.

Madani declined to name the tanker but said it was not under US Treasury sanctions and had entered the region without drawing scrutiny. The Reuters report gave no destination for the cargo or indication that other tankers were preparing to sail.

In a commentary on Thursday, the Revolutionary Guards-affiliated Fars news agency urged Tehran to send a tanker convoy to China, arguing that the prospect of Iranian retaliation against oil terminals in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar could deter Washington from firing on the tankers.

Sabereen News said Tehran had warned governments across the region that it would go to war if the United States attacked Iranian tankers sailing to China.

Energy analyst Abdollah Babakhani wrote on social media that Iran could retaliate against ports and oil terminals in the region if the United States attacked or seized Iranian tankers attempting to cross the blockade.

He said the region appeared to be on the verge of a period of intense but possibly short-lived tension.
